q: Is the reachability deficit at low p an ansatz-expressibility limit, an optimizer-landscape failure (local minima / barren-plateau shallow-gradient region), or both? Our COBYLA + 4-restart sweep cannot distinguish these — a stuck optimizer inflates f above the true reachability minimum.
basis: The paper argues the deficit is genuinely a manifold-coverage property of the X-mixer QAOA state family, but never reports optimizer robustness checks. Since 2019 the literature (McClean 2018 barren plateaus, Larocca 2022 theory of overparameterization, Wang 2021 noise-induced BP) has made this an active question, and Akshay et al. do not disentangle the two effects in 1906.11259.
next_steps: Re-run our α∈{2,3,5,7,10} × p∈{1,2,4} cells with three optimizers (COBYLA, L-BFGS-B with analytic gradients from the statevector, BOBYQA), 20 random restarts each, and record the spread of best-of-restarts f. If f converges across optimizers → expressibility limit confirmed. If L-BFGS-B / more restarts systematically lowers f → part of the deficit is optimizer failure. Cost: ~10× current sweep (~1.5 hr CPU on CherryRd). Free.

q: Do warm-start QAOA (Egger et al. 2020) or ADAPT-QAOA (Zhu et al. 2022) close the reachability deficit at the same low p on the paper's exact instance family, or does the α-dependence survive the more expressive ansatz?
basis: 1906.11259 predates both variants. If the deficit is fundamentally about the constraint density (a problem property) rather than the ansatz (an algorithm property), it should persist across ADAPT/warm-start. If it is ansatz-specific, ADAPT should erase it at large α. Nobody has (to our knowledge) run this head-to-head on the same 3-SAT instance ensemble the paper studies.
next_steps: Extend qaoa_reachability.py with (a) a warm-start init using a classical relaxation (GW or greedy 3-SAT) as γ0/β0, and (b) an ADAPT-QAOA driver that greedily grows the ansatz from a mixer pool {X_i, X_iX_j} up to p_max=4 operators. Same 15 instances/α, α∈{1,3,5,7,10}. Compare f_deficit head-to-head. CPU-only, free. Est. 4-6 hr on m1.

q: How does hardware noise (single-qubit depolarizing, T1/T2, readout) interact with the reachability deficit? Does noise make the deficit larger (worse expressibility once the state is mixed) or does noise-induced concentration flatten the landscape enough to accidentally reduce f?
basis: The paper is pure noiseless statevector. Post-2019 work (França & García-Patrón 2021 on limitations of noisy QAOA, Marshall et al. 2020 on characterizing local noise) suggests that even 0.1% two-qubit gate error can dominate the effective reachability for p>10. No published study has computed the noisy analog of Fig.~1 on the same random-3-SAT ensemble.
next_steps: Add a density-matrix backend (qiskit-aer or a from-scratch superoperator layer for n=6, dim=64×64 fits easily) with per-gate depolarizing p_1=1e-4, p_2=1e-3 and readout error 1e-2. Re-run p∈{4,8} across α at n=6. Compare (i) noiseless f, (ii) noisy f_min, (iii) noisy-then-post-selected f. Free (CPU statevector/density-matrix at n=6).

q: Can the reachability deficit at large α be predicted from a structural feature of individual 3-SAT instances (backbone size, community structure of the factor graph, average clause overlap) rather than from α alone? Fig.~1 shows large per-instance spread hidden inside the mean — what explains that spread?
basis: The paper reports means and error bars but does not correlate per-instance f with any structural descriptor. Our per-instance JSON (qaoa_3sat_sweep.json) contains 15 individual f values per (α,p) cell — enough to fit a regression against instance-level features. If a single structural feature explains most of the within-α variance, the reachability-deficit story becomes richer than 'α is what matters'.
next_steps: For each of our 15×7 = 105 instances, compute (a) backbone size via exhaustive SAT enumeration (n=6, cheap), (b) factor-graph diameter/average degree, (c) fraction of clauses sharing ≥2 variables, (d) unit-propagation depth. Regress log(f_instance) at p=4 against these features. Report R² per feature and the strongest predictor. Pure post-processing on existing data, zero new sims. <1 hr.

q: Do alternative mixers (XY-mixer, ring mixer, Grover-like reflection mixer) change the α-dependence of the deficit, or is the α-scaling universal across mixer choices? The paper tests one alternative (projector driver, Fig. 2) and reports 'similar' behavior but at different p — is that quantitative similarity or just qualitative?
basis: The paper's Fig.~2 shows the projector mixer 'also exhibits reachability deficits but needs lower p for comparable f.' The comparison is presented without a joint plot, so it's hard to tell whether the α-scaling exponent is truly the same or just visually similar. Modern mixer-design work (Hadfield et al. QAOA→QAOA+, Bärtschi & Eidenbenz 2020 grover mixers) makes this a live question.
next_steps: Add 3 mixers to qaoa_reachability.py: (i) standard X (already there), (ii) XY-mixer exp(-iβ Σ (X_iX_{i+1}+Y_iY_{i+1})), (iii) Grover reflection 2|+⟩⟨+|-I. Fix p=4, sweep α∈{1,3,5,7,10}, 15 instances each, plot f_mean vs α with three curves. Fit log-log slope in the α∈[3,10] regime; report whether the slope is mixer-invariant (universal) or mixer-dependent. Free, ~2 hr CPU.
